transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-21 16:00 UTC | Duration 54m
Attendees: Samantha Lee (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood Solutions); Ellen Park (Head of ML, NewWave), Ravi Patel (Platform Eng), Marta Silva (CTO), Jonas Berg (SRE)

Auto-summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and prefix/KV cache cost model. Demo of Console recommendations and a quick cost calc. Next steps: pricing, bench spreadsheets, traffic sample, schedule POC.

00:00 Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a 45-ish minute walkthrough of Redwood Optimize — focusing on batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations given the payment use case. Fell free to interrupt.
00:18 Ellen: Thanks, Samantha. We're mainly concerned about per-transaction latency for customer support chat and some batch reconciliation jobs. Also want to understand cost implications.
00:32 Carlos: Great, so quick agenda — batching strategies, prefix vs KV cache, show the cost model in the console, and then some recommended configs for your traffic shape.
00:48 Marta: Quick Q — we ran a pilot with another provider and they flattened latency a lot but cost was unexpectedly high at scale. Hoping to see tradeoffs.
01:05 Carlos: Totally. We'll show a couple of knobs: target latency SLO, batching window, max tokens per batch, and cache hit-rate assumptions.
01:22 Ravi: Our traffic is spiky — spike to 400 TPS during peak, baseline 60 TPS. Most prompts are short, 40-80 tokens, but we have a set of long-context reconciliation prompts ~800 tokens.
01:40 Carlos: Perfect, that's the mix we wanted to see. For short chat messages, continuous batching with a small batching window (10-25ms) often gives good unit cost without hurting p95 latency. For reconciliation, you want to avoid coalescing long-context requests with short ones because memory and KV-cache behavior differs.
02:05 Samantha: I'll pull up the console. (screen share) Here's the Optimize tab — it suggests batching profile A for low-latency chat and profile B for higher throughput reconciliation. Note the estimated tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens.
02:28 Carlos: Important to call out: prefix cache vs KV cache. Prefix caching stores recurrent prefixes of prompts — good for templates and system messages. KV cache stores model key-value activations for longer sessions, which is great for long context where you want to avoid recomputing earlier tokens.
02:50 Ellen: Which gives better cost savings typically?
03:00 Carlos: Short answer: prefix caching is higher hit-rate for templated messages and is cheap to maintain — big wins for chatbots. KV cache gives bigger wins for long sessions, especially with autoregressive decoding where early tokens are stable. But KV cache memory and eviction policies matter — that's where our cost model helps.
03:25 Samantha: Let me show the cost model we ran for a 1M prompts sample. (shares spreadsheet link) We assumed: average short prompt 60 tokens, response 30 tokens; long prompt 800 tokens, response 600 tokens; 75% of traffic short, 25% long; KV cache hit 40% on long sessions after tuning, prefix cache hit 55% on short templates.
03:55 Carlos: With those numbers, unit cost falls by roughly 18-28% using prefix caching for chat and additional 12-20% using KV cache in reconciliation workloads — depending on hit rates and batch sizing.
04:20 Jonas: Are those numbers accounting for dedicated pool pricing vs hosted?
04:30 Samantha: The console shows both. Hosted per-token baseline and then a dedicated reserved capacity BOM which amortizes GPU cost but requires commit. For 400 TPS peaks, we recommended a small dedicated pool plus hosted fallback to avoid throttling under heavy spikes.
04:55 Ravi: How do fallbacks work? If dedicated is saturated will requests route to a compatible model variant?
05:05 Carlos: Yes — smart routing will fallback to compatible smaller quantized variant if policy allows. You can set per-route policy: strict (no fallback) vs best-effort (allow quantized fallback). We'll show the config.
05:22 Samantha: Quick detour to security, Marta?
05:27 Marta: Yes, we need VPC deployment and KMS integration — any PII must not leave our region. Also SOC2 and audit logs.
05:36 Priya: Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem options and KMS/HSM integrations; audit logs are available via the Console and can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll attach the SOC2 doc.
05:50 Marta: Good. For latency-sensitive traffic we also need predictable egress and compliance with data residency.
06:02 Carlos: Noted — when we model cost we can use regional pricing and dedicated node amortization per your region.
06:15 Samantha: Back to batching. Here's an example config: for chat route, batching window 20ms, max batch size 64 tokens per request, prefer small quantized variant for lower priority routes. For reconciliation, batch window 80ms, max batch 8 requests because each request is heavy.
06:40 Carlos: Also show the Optimize console's predicted p50/p95 under these settings. (shares chart) Chat p95 under 20ms window stays under 220ms, p99 ~420ms; reconciliation p95 around 1.2s given long context.
07:05 Ellen: That p99 is a little high for chat — our target p95 is 200ms, p99 350ms. Can we tune?
07:15 Carlos: You can trade cost for latency by reducing batching window or reserving more dedicated capacity. Reducing the window to 10ms drops p95 by ~30ms but increases per-token cost by about 6-8% in our model.
07:35 Marta: Pricing that out — what would that look like monthly?
07:40 Samantha: For your traffic shape (baseline 60 TPS, spikes to 400 TPS, mix earlier), projected monthly cost hosted-only ~ $18k/month with current model assumptions. Mixed dedicated + hosted fallback with reserved commitment (small pool) brings it to ~$12k/month amortized but with a 6-12 month commit. Exact numbers in the spreadsheet.
08:05 Ravi: The difference seems meaningful but commits are a blocker for us. We might try a short pilot.
08:12 Samantha: That's why we suggest a 30-day pilot with a small dedicated pool to prove savings, then decide on commit.
08:20 Carlos: Now, caching specifics — prefix cache eviction TTLs, granularity: store user/system prefixes only for templated messages; avoid storing PII in prefix. We have filters.
08:38 Ellen: For long reconciliation sessions, how large will KV cache grow per session?
08:45 Carlos: For an 800-token context, KV cache will be roughly proportional to model hidden dimension and layers — in our 8k context model that equates to ~X MB per session (transcription: 'like 40MB' was said — typically depends on quantization) — but you'll want to cap per-session cache TTL and evict after 30m of inactivity to manage memory.
09:12 Jonas: What's the memory overhead per dedicated node?
09:18 Carlos: Depends on model/quantization. In our cost model example we used a 16GB GPU that can hold about 4 concurrent long sessions with KV cache; you can increase concurrency by using quantized kernels or more nodes. We'll include exact node breakdown in the spreadsheet.
09:36 Samantha: Let's walk through an example cost calc for 1M requests — quick numbers: baseline hosted tokens cost = $X (screen: shows numbers). With prefix cache hit 55% you drop token compute by ~25% for chat. With KV cache hit on long sessions at 40% you drop heavy token recompute by ~30% for that bucket. Combined result shows overall token compute reduction ~22%.
10:10 Ellen: Any impact on model quality from quantized variants used as fallback?
10:18 Carlos: Slight degradation possible — we recommend A/B tests for critical prompts. The Console's eval tooling can run regressions tied to prompt sets and alert on quality regression.
10:30 Marta: Ok, security follow-up — send SOC2 and encryption-at-rest docs.
10:36 Priya: We'll attach them.
10:40 Samantha: A couple practical recommendations for NewWave: 1) start with two routes: low-latency chat (small window, prefix cache aggressive), high-throughput reconciliation (larger window, KV cache), 2) configure routing fallback to allow quantized variant for non-critical paths, 3) pilot a small dedicated pool for peak shaving.
11:05 Ravi: Sounds good. For the pilot can you also run a benchmark with our sample traffic?
11:10 Carlos: Yes — we'll run a baseline with your traffic, measure p95/p99 and cost per million tokens, and return a bench report. We'll need the 72h sample and any secrets redacted.
11:28 Ellen: Timeline?
11:30 Samantha: We'll compile pricing + BOM by EOD Tuesday (2026-03-24), Carlos will share bench scripts by Monday (2026-03-23). Pilot kickoff asap after we ingest traffic.
11:50 Marta: One more — auditing: can we forward logs to Splunk?
11:55 Priya: Yes, audit logs can stream to your SIEM; we'll add the runbook.
12:05 Samantha: Ok we'll recap next steps.
12:12 Carlos: Recap: share pricing, share bench scripts, customer to provide traffic, schedule poc check-in 2026-04-01.
12:25 Ellen: Great, thanks. Quick note — also evaluate tokenization differences across models; we had surprises earlier.
12:35 Carlos: We'll include tokenizer parity checks in the bench.
12:45 Samantha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

End of transcript.

Artifacts shared: https://redwood.app/sheets/kv-cache-bench-99234 (spreadsheet), https://redwood.app/docs/soc2.pdf (security), screenshot links in console during demo.

Notes on transcription quality: speaker labels sometimes generic, occasional word swaps (e.g., "eight K context" transcribed as "ate K context").
